name: Furazabol
lead: Furazabol is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid that has been marketed in Japan since 1969. It is a 17α-alkylated derivative of dihydrotestosterone and is structurally close to stanozolol, differing in having a furazan ring where stanozolol has a pyrazole ring.[1] People in strength and physique circles who discuss anabolic steroids in general are interested in compounds of this class because they promote muscle protein synthesis and lean mass, which changes how muscular a body looks; furazabol itself is rarely discussed in these communities and has been used mainly in Japanese clinical practice.

Wikipedia reports a relatively high anabolic-to-androgenic ratio and describes antihyperlipidemic properties, which the author William Llewellyn regards as a myth.[1] Published sources on furazabol are largely animal pharmacology and analytical studies for doping control rather than human efficacy trials.[2][3]
In North America furazabol became known through the Dubin Inquiry into the 1988 Olympic doping case of sprinter Ben Johnson, who said he had been taking it.[1][11]

paras: Furazabol was developed as a medical anabolic agent and has been marketed in Japan since 1969, with brand names including Frazalon and Miotalon.[1] Wikipedia describes reported antihyperlipidemic properties, and early Japanese studies examined non-hormonal effects such as fibrinolysis and cholesterol handling in animals.[1][5][6][12]

In appearance terms, the interest in 17α-alkylated anabolic steroids is that they act on androgen receptors in muscle. Furazabol is described as having a relatively high anabolic-to-androgenic ratio, though that figure comes from animal-type assays and has not been confirmed in physique studies in humans.[1]

Like other anabolic-androgenic steroids, furazabol acts as an androgen receptor agonist. A 1980 rat study found that furazabol, among other anabolic steroids, altered the level of cytosolic androgen receptor in the prostate of castrated animals.[7]

Early Japanese work described the metabolites of furazabol in rats and some non-hormonal properties of the compound.[4][5] A 1976 rat study reported that treatment enhanced fibrinolytic and thrombolytic potential.[6][13] A 1972 study examined influences of testosterone, progesterone and furazabol on the cholesterol-shifting response to estrone.[12]

Wikipedia lists a half-life of about four hours, noting the figure lacks a citation.[1] Metabolism includes 17-epimerization, as with other 17α-methyl anabolic steroids.[10] Human urine excretion studies were later published for doping control.[8][9]

Like other 17α-alkylated anabolic steroids, furazabol may carry a risk of hepatotoxicity.[1] Stanozolol, its closest relative, is described in Wikipedia as associated with virilization, liver toxicity, cardiovascular disease and hypertension, and the same class concerns are generally discussed for related compounds.[14]

Furazabol has the formula C20H30N2O2.[1] It is a 17α-methyl DHT derivative with a furazan ring fused to the A ring, whereas stanozolol carries a pyrazole ring at the same position.[1][14] Its chemical name is 17β-hydroxy-17α-methyl-5α-androstano[2,3-c]furazan, as used in the early Japanese papers.[4]

Furazabol has been marketed in Japan since 1969.[1] Early Japanese pharmaceutical research in the early 1970s documented its metabolism and non-hormonal effects.[4][5] Stanozolol, by contrast, was developed by Sterling-Winthrop in 1962 and sold as Winstrol and Stromba; the IOC and IAAF first banned synthetic steroids, including stanozolol, in 1974.[14]

In North America, furazabol was little known to athletes until the Dubin Inquiry. After winning the 100 m at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, Ben Johnson tested positive for stanozolol and was stripped of his medal. He later claimed to have been taking furazabol, which he said could not be detected. His physician testified that he supplied furazabol, but a vial that sprinter Angella Issajenko believed held furazabol proved to contain stanozolol. The Commission concluded that stanozolol had been supplied and that furazabol was either imagined or a fabrication.[1] Charles Dubin, Chief Justice of the Ontario Court of Appeal, led the inquiry in 1989 and released his report in June 1990 with more than 70 recommendations, writing that doping threatened the essential integrity of sport.[11]
Furazabol is Schedule III in the US and Schedule IV in Canada.[1]

Analytical chemistry papers have described detection of furazabol metabolites in human urine and in racehorse doping tests.[3][8][9] Screening methods developed for stanozolol are discussed in the context of improving detection for related steroids.[2]
No studies found of furazabol for muscle or appearance outcomes. Available research consists of rat pharmacology and doping-detection studies in humans and horses.[3][6][8]

chain: Claimed gains in lean mass and strength
angle.text: Furazabol is an oral anabolic steroid of the stanozolol family that has been sold as a medicine in Japan since 1969. Its anabolic profile is why it is discussed in the doping literature; no human trials have measured physique outcomes.

card.summary: Oral Japanese anabolic steroid, close cousin of stanozolol, best known in the West from the Ben Johnson doping inquiry; no modern human trials.
card.note: 17α-alkylated steroid with possible liver toxicity; controlled in the US (Schedule III) and Canada (Schedule IV).

quick.overview:
Furazabol is an oral anabolic-androgenic steroid marketed in Japan since 1969. Structurally it is nearly identical to stanozolol, with a furazan ring in place of stanozolol's pyrazole ring.
It is rarely discussed outside doping history. No modern human trial of its effect on muscle or appearance exists; the available research is mostly doping-control and animal studies.
quick.mechanism: It is a 17α-alkylated derivative of dihydrotestosterone and acts on the androgen receptor. It is reported to have a relatively high ratio of anabolic to androgenic activity. Rat studies also reported effects on blood fibrinolysis, and it has been described as lipid-lowering.
quick.risks: As a 17α-alkylated steroid it may carry a risk of liver toxicity. It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the United States and Schedule IV in Canada, and anabolic steroids are prohibited in sport.
